The Pencil language

What exists today. decisions.md has why each part is the way it is. A test in crates/pencil-core/tests/language_doc.rs fails if a built-in function, style property or statement goes undocumented here. The syntax can still change freely (goals.md), so treat this as a description of the current language, not a promise.

The corpus in corpus/ has working examples of everything below.

Documents

A .pen file is a list of statements. Comments run from // to the end of the line. Style rules can sit in the document or in separate style files.

Values can be written after they’re used. A let, fn, param, choice or solve used before it’s written is worked out just before its first use, so a figure can say what it draws first and how its values are found after. What’s drawn keeps the order it’s written in, which is what’s on top, and so does the timeline. A curve, circle or line used as a value, such as in intersect(c, l, 0), is something drawn, so it comes first. A value defined in terms of itself, through others or not, is an error. A beat’s name can be read before its beat is written too. Beats and pauses can’t pass each other, so they stay in order, and a beat with a block holds marks, which stay where they are, so only a beat without one can be read early.

A figure can be more than one file. use "limacon/mirror.pen" puts that file’s statements where the line is, as if they were written there. Everything is still one figure with one set of names, so a part can show, drop or move what another part drew, and a name defined twice is an error wherever the two are.

  • The path is from the file that says it, with / between folders and .. to step out of one: use "arms.pen" in limacon/mirror.pen is limacon/arms.pen. A path can’t start at a root or be a URL.
  • A file joins once. A second use of it adds nothing, so two parts can each use the helpers they need.
  • A file can’t use itself, directly or through another.
  • A used file is whole statements, so a beat { … } block can’t open in one file and close in another. It can be a figure by itself too: its doc name is ignored when it’s used.
  • A sheet can use files the same way, for names and functions several sheets share.
  • An error says which file it’s in, with the line in that file: limacon/mirror.pen:12:3: unknown name ….

The core never opens a file. The command reads them from disk, and <pencil-figure> fetches them from beside the file that names them. lab/explainer/limacon.pen is the example: a file to each part of its story.

Statement Meaning
doc name Names the document.
duration 13 How long one pass of the time bindings takes, for looping and video. Any constant will do (see Constants): duration 2·π loops once per turn of time. An expression reads it as duration.
poster { time: 3.5, roll: 0.6 } The moment a still of the figure shows: a time, and params held at values, as a reader could set them. A build draws it for a page to show until the figure runs (see Posters).
viewport { … } The world window (see below).
let x = expr A named value: a number, point, circle or line.
fn f(a, b) = expr A function, inlined where it’s called. No recursion.
param a = 1 in 0..2·π A root that time or a reader can drive. It stays in its range however it’s driven: its default, a binding, a reader’s control and a drag all stop at the range’s ends.
param p = 2 in 0..q step 1 A range whose end follows other params, here one that says p can’t pass q. An end is numbers, constants (see Constants), and params, declared before or after it: not a let that a param or time moves, a choice’s value or time. The figure keeps p inside the range as it stands each frame, so a reader who lowers q below p brings p down with it. What the reader set isn’t lost: raise q again and p goes back to it. A page reads the widest the range gets and which params move it (info.params: min, max, follows), and the range as it stands (figure.range("p")), so a control built from them stops where the figure does. The widest is found at the ends of the ranges it reads, which is right for an end that only rises or falls with each. A range that ends before it starts leaves its start.
param n = 3 in 1..12 step 1 A param that only takes its range’s start plus whole steps, however it’s driven: its default, a binding, a reader or a drag goes to the nearest one. A step of 1 makes it a whole number, and a page’s control steps the same way. The step is a constant (see Constants).
param axis in {ω, 1, 1 + ω} A param that’s one of these values, the first unless = 1 names another as written. They can be any one kind, and numbers go with points as points on the real axis. The name is the chosen value, so the math can use it directly: imag(conj(axis)·P) is the cross product with whichever direction was chosen. The param a reader sets is axis.index, which option it is, from 0, and a page labels each option with its text, or with its name: in {"p = 0": 2·π / q, "q = 2p": …} a page shows the names and the math gets the values, and = "q = 2p" starts there.
param q "arms" = 8 in 3..16 step 1 A caption, after the name, as a beat’s is: what the param’s control on a page says, in words. A choice takes one the same way, param along "direction" in {1, i, 1 + i}. Without one, a control says the param’s name (see Controls and readouts).
solve (x, y) from 0, 1: f(x, y) = 0, g(x, y) = 2 Unknowns defined by equations (see below).
bind a = expr What drives a param when no reader has taken it over. A param with a binding has two drivers, the binding and the reader, and the reader’s last action picks. Setting it, with a drag, a key, a control or a page’s hold, takes it over. Setting a param its binding reads, directly, through other bindings, a choice’s options or a range, hands it back: in bind theta = case, where the case’s options read q, setting q or the case brings θ back to its binding. Params set together, as in the element’s params="q: 8; theta: 1", keep each other. Time is the same: setting it, or playing, hands back what it drives. A page reads which params each binding reads in info.params (reads), and needs no script of its own for this.
beat "caption" tag t { … } A discrete step of a construction (see below).
beat spin "caption" for 2 show P drop c focus P, .arms One move of a figure’s story (see below). A named one can leave for 2 out, and takes a second.
pause 0.4 A hold between moves, in seconds, a constant (see Constants).
curve c = … A drawn curve, in one of the forms below.
segment s = A, B A straight line between points.
path p = A, B, C An open line through points.
polygon p = A, B, C A closed line through points.
rightangle m = A, V, B size 0.2 A right-angle mark at V, a world size along each side.
region r = A, f(t) for t in 0..1 A filled area bounded by points and arcs.
dot P, Q Draws point bindings. A dot takes its point’s name, so a style can target it.
label n = "−{q}" at P away D Text at a point, on the side D points to, in the figure’s own coordinates. Its style’s distance says how far. {expr} in the text is a value: a number, written to the style’s digits and whole if it’s whole, or a point, written as its style’s format says. $…$ in the text is mathematics, laid out (see Mathematics in labels). What a label says about a value is its style’s text. Without text, each panel gives it (see Panels). A figure without panels needs text, unless the label is a value’s.
label root at P A label named after a value is that value’s label, as a dot is its point’s, so one rule styles both. It’s about that value, and its style’s text says what it shows of it: with no text of its own, the value. A value has one label. A label whose text is one value, "{q - 1}", is about that value in the same way.
label n = "P" at P offset (12, -12) The same, at a fixed shift in px with y down. A sheet can’t change it, so prefer away.
label ratio = "ratio {q / p}", label k A label with no place is a readout: said as text beside the figure, and not drawn in it, with everything a label has (see Controls and readouts).
arrow v = A, B A shaft and a head, as one line.
dots d = P(i) for i in 1..n with z = f(i) One mark drawn many times (see below).
circles c = circle(C(i), T(i)) for i in 1..n The same, as circles.
curves c = parametric (t): P(t, i) for t in a..b for i in 1..n The same, as curves.
curves h = parametric (t): (±cosh(t), sinh(t)) for t in -2..2 Both signs: a collection with ± draws each instance twice, the + branch first (see Collections).
dots d = (i, s) for i in 0..n, s in {-1, 1} A variable over a list, in the order written (see Collections).
group g(k) { … } Things to draw in more than one place, declared once in their own coordinates.
use g(2), use g(2) through f as up Draws a group here, optionally through a function and under a prefix (see Panels).
use "parts/mirror.pen" Another file’s statements, here (see Documents).
text n = "1" What a label says in this panel (see Panels).
outline o = detail The rectangle another panel is looking at.
panel p "Title" { … } One view of the figure, with its own marks (see below).
place p = P offset (8, 18) hang end Where an expression can sit (see below).
expression e { on grow: … } A list of states whose matching parts move, each reached on the beat it names (see below).
expression e by step { … } The same, with a number saying which state it’s in.
handle P sets a = expr Dragging P sets param a to expr, the inverse from the pointer to the param, written out. expr can use pointer.x and pointer.y, and pointer by itself is the pointer’s point, so abs(pointer) is its distance from the origin and real(ln(pointer)) the log of that. a takes the value within its range and step, which is what constrains the drag. Dragging, or the keys on the handle, take a over from its binding, until a param that binding reads is set (see bind). The handle is a’s control: the site’s controls give a param a handle sets no slider.
handle z sets a = expr, b = expr A point dragged in two dimensions: dragging z sets two params, each to its own expression, which can use the pointer as above. For let z = a + b·i it’s a = pointer.x, b = pointer.y, and for a point on a lattice, z = a + b·ω, the two expressions turn the pointer into its coefficients: a = pointer.x - pointer.y·real(ω)/imag(ω), b = pointer.y/imag(ω). Both are worked out from the same pointer and the params as they were, then each param takes its value within its own range and step, so at the end of one range that param stops and the other goes on. One drag sets both, so they don’t hand each other back. Arrow keys move the point on the page through the same expressions, and Home, End, Page Up and Page Down are long moves left, right, up and down. A key’s move stays within 45° of its way, going on to a param’s next step if it has to, so on a slanted lattice Up is never mostly Left, and a key with no such move, as along the edge of a range, does nothing. Two at most, each a param, each named once. A mark has one handle: a second on the same mark is an error, since a drag takes one, so a point dragged in two dimensions is one handle setting both. The check goes by name, so two names for one point, let w = z with dot z, w, can each have a handle, and a drag takes the nearer, or the later where they’re the same point.
style selector { … } A style rule (see below).
tag a, b After a statement, tags the marks it made.

Curve forms

Each form keeps its own representation (goals.md).

Form Example Drawn by default
Implicit curve c = implicit (x, y): x² + y² = r² Traced to a line
Exact distance curve c = sdf (x, y): sqrt(x² + y²) - r Per pixel
Parametric curve c = parametric (t): (cos(t), sin(t)) for t in 0..2·π Sampled to a line
Construction curve c = circle(O, A), curve g = ray(O, B) A circle per pixel, a line or ray as a line

An implicit curve is traced on a grid of cells 6 device pixels across, and the line is kept within a quarter of a pixel of the curve both ways. Where the curve bends sharper than a cell, as at each tip of sin(30·x) = y, the line is bent onto it, and where two parts of the curve pass through one cell, the cell is split in four, down to a sixteenth of a cell, so a tip is drawn to its point and two arms that run close stay apart until they’re under about half a pixel apart. A curve with more detail than that, as one zoomed far out, is followed as far as a budget for each frame goes, a few times the grid’s own work, spent where the line strays furthest first, and past it the line is left as the grid finds it, with tips cut short and near parts joined. Nothing says when that happens. Every point the line is drawn through is on the curve, also where the expression levels off around it, as tanh(50·(x² + y² - 1)) = 0 does, and where it falls to zero as a cube root does, as across the vertical tangent of y = sign(x)·abs(x)^(1/3).

An implicit curve is where its expression is zero, so where the expression changes sign without going through zero, across a pole or a jump, nothing is traced: y = tan(x) is its branches with nothing along x = ±π/2, and y = floor(x) is steps without risers. The line stops at the edge of the grid cell the pole or the jump runs through. Where a curve runs along its asymptote, within a cell of the pole, that can be a long stretch, and writing the curve without the pole, x·y = 1 for y = 1/x, draws it whole.

A parametric range can run down as well as up, and the curve is drawn from its first bound, so for u in 0..t sweeps an angle from 0 to t whichever sign t has. trim and a head follow that direction. A collection’s for i in a..b counts up, and is empty when b is below a.

A range can be written med ± dev, the tolerance reading of ±, as in x = 5 ± 2: it’s (med - abs(dev))..(med + abs(dev)), anywhere a range is written, the interval between its two values whichever is larger, so a negative dev never reverses it. for k in 2 ± 1 counts 1, 2 and 3, for t in 0 ± π runs from −π to π, param a = 1 in 1 ± 0.5 step 0.25 steps through 0.5 to 1.5, and viewport { x: 0 ± 2 } is -2..2. It’s only a spelling: each place takes what it takes of a range’s ends, and it doesn’t make a collection two branches, so for k in 2 ± 1 has no self.sign. It’s the whole range or nothing. ±x alone would be the two values +x and −x, so it’s an error that offers {x, -x} for those and -x..x or 0 ± x for the interval. ∓ isn’t a range, and a ± in one end of a range, 0..(2 ± 1), would make two ranges: with both signs, count over them first, for s in {1, -1}, k in 0..(2 + s).

Viewport

viewport { x: -2..2, y: -2..2 }

  • x, y: a fixed world window, as -2..2 or 0 ± 2. It always has one scale for both axes, so at a different shape it shows more, rather than stretching. Its bounds are constants (see Constants), so they can’t read time or a param. To follow something that moves, fit it.
  • fit: a b c: bounds these points and circles each frame instead of a fixed window, ignoring any param a handle has taken over, so a drag doesn’t rescale the figure under the pointer.
  • pad: 0.04: extra space around a fit, as a fraction of its size. A constant (see Constants).
  • yaw: 0.45·roll: how far the view is turned about its vertical axis, for points in space (see Points in space). It can read params and time, so a view can turn as a figure plays.

A viewport says what part of the plane the figure shows, and not how big it’s drawn. That depends on where it’s drawn, so it’s a sheet’s: style figure { width: 640px; height: 400px } (see Styles). The same figure can be 16:9 in a video’s sheet and fit a page’s column in another’s.

Posters

A still of a figure stands in for it where it can’t run, or hasn’t started: on a page before its first frame, in a link’s preview, in print. A figure knows which moment tells the most, and it’s a binding of time and params like any other, so the document says:

poster { time: 3.5, roll: 0.6 }

  • time is a moment of the clock, and anything else is a param, held there as if a reader had set it. Each is a constant (see Constants), so time: duration / 5 is a fifth of the way through.
  • A param that follows time is held, or time is said, and not both. Time and a reader take turns on such a param, and a poster is one moment: time gives the param the value it has there, so holding it as well is an error. A param time doesn’t drive goes with a time, as roll does above.
  • Without one, the poster is the end of the story for a figure whose beats are moves, where everything has arrived, and the start of the clock for any other.
  • It changes nothing about the figure as it runs. A page that wants the figure to start where its poster is holds those params itself, from what the build wrote down.

pencil build DOC.pen --style … --out DIR draws it, at the figure’s design size and at twice it, as PNG and, where it’s smaller, as WebP, beside the compiled figure and a .json of what a page needs to know: the figure’s shape, its duration, its params with their ranges, its beats and captions, its poster’s moment with every param’s value and range there, the colors its sheets name, and every file that went into it (sources), so a build knows when to make it again. --card adds a 1200×630 card for sharing, the figure on its own paper. The Astro component in packages/figure runs this for each figure on a site, and writes the page around what it made.

Controls and readouts

A page can show a figure’s controls beside it: a play button and time, beat stepping, a control for each param a handle doesn’t set, and the readouts. Their words are the document’s, written where they belong, and a sheet says how much of them to say, as it does for a label.

A param’s caption is what its control says: param q "arms" = 8 in 3..16 step 1, after the name, where a beat writes its caption. A choice takes one the same way: param along "direction" in {1, i, 1 + i}, and param along "direction" = "i" in {…} with a default. Without one, a control says the param’s name, set as mathematics.

  • It’s words. A value changes, so it’s a readout’s, and a caption with {…} in it is an error. So is one with $…$, which a control can’t set yet: write the symbol, as "θ".
  • Each param gets the control that fits it. A range is a slider, with its value after it. A choice of a few options, four at most, is radios, which show every option at once, and a choice of more is a list that opens. A choice of off and on, two options written 0 and 1 or named off and on, as in param glow in {"off": 0, "on": 1}, is a checkbox. A param a handle sets has no control of its own: the handle is its control.

A label with no place is a readout: label ratio = "ratio {q / p}", or label k for a value. It’s said as text beside the figure, after the controls, and isn’t drawn in it. It has everything a label has: {expr} values, $…$ mathematics, a sheet’s digits, a point’s format and text. With no text in its sheets it says which value it is, since beside the figure nothing else does: a value’s name and value, k = 0.62 for label k, and q − 1 = 2 for label n = "{q - 1}", as text: name = value says them, or its own words with its value, ratio = 2.67 for label r = "ratio", and words with values in them as they’re written.

  • It’s the whole figure’s, so it’s written among the figure’s own statements, not in a group, which can be drawn more than once, or in a panel. A figure with panels says its readouts beside all of them.
  • It’s tagged readout, and its type is label, so style readout { digits: 3 } reaches every one, and style label reaches them with the labels.
  • One that doesn’t exist this frame says —.
  • A screen reader hears its mathematics as mathematics: $z^2 = 1$ is “z squared = 1”, x_1 “x sub 1”, (a + b)/2 “(a + b) over 2” and sqrt(x) “the square root of x”.
  • A page keeps room for it, as wide and as tall as the most it says, worked out from the moments a reader can reach: the poster’s, and the one a build or a page starts the figure at, with the params it holds; moments through the clock from there; each param through its range, at each of its steps if it has a few and at nine places along it otherwise; and every param at its start or its end together. Every number is counted as written to its digits, a whole one too, and each digit as a wide one. A value that only gets wider between those can say more than the room, and its box keeps its size anyway, so nothing beside it moves.
  • It’s only said beside a figure on a page. pencil render, svg and video draw what’s in the figure, and leave readouts out, as a page’s controls are.

A sheet says what a control says, and which control it is, as for a thing whose type is control and whose name is its param’s: style control { … } is every control, and style q.control { … } is q’s, or for a choice, the name its value has, along.control. A param’s name alone, style q, still names a mark. So control is taken: nothing in a figure can be called or tagged it, and that’s an error that says so.

Property Meaning
text What the control says, as a label’s text: caption (its caption, or its name if it has none), name, and value, said after a slider. text: caption = value is the default, text: name = value says q, and text: caption leaves the value out. A choice shows its option in the control itself.
kind Which control it is: slider, radios, select or checkbox. Any param can be a slider, a choice radios or a select, and a choice of off and on a checkbox. A rule for every control sets a kind only on those it fits, and one that names a control has to fit it.

<pencil-figure controls> shows them, and a build writes them into the page before any script runs (the package’s README).

Beats

There are two kinds of beat, and a figure’s are all one kind. A step is beat "caption" { … }: a block with a caption, and no name and no length. A move is a beat with a name, a length, or both: beat grow, beat grow for 1, beat "A circle." for 1.

A step groups marks into a discrete stage of a construction. Any beat declares the param beat, ranging over the beats, and a step’s marks get the block’s tags. A self.age in a style is that mark’s own beat − index, so one rule can fade every earlier step. In a figure with a duration, steps share it evenly and beat follows time, so the timing is said once: ten steps in duration 30 are 3 s each. With no duration, a reader steps through them. bind beat = … can still drive them by something else. A step has no progress: beat is a whole number, and what a step shows is there all at once.

A beat can say what it’s about, a move or a step: focus P, .arms, and self.focus is 1 on those during that beat and 0 on the rest, until a beat names others. An entry can follow a choice, so the beat is about what a reader picked: focus level, .boundary if case = "p = 0", .middle if case = "q = 2p". On a step, focus comes after its tags: beat "…" tag t focus … {.

A move is one move of a figure’s story, and takes time. Beats and pauses run in the order they’re written, and their lengths add up to the duration, so making one longer moves everything after it instead of everything having to be retimed. A length is a constant (see Constants):

pause 0.4
beat grow "A circle." for 1 show c
beat spin "A point goes round." for 2 show P focus P
pause 1
beat gone for 0.5 drop c, P
  • beat is a number, whole while the figure holds and between two whole numbers while a beat moves: 1.5 is halfway through the second beat. Time drives it, and a reader stepping through or a bind beat can drive it instead, and everything below follows.
  • A beat’s name is its progress, 0 until it starts, 1 once it’s done, and moving evenly in between. So let r = grow grows with that beat, and snap(grow) eases it. It’s a number like any other, so when two things follow one beat, ease it once and have both read that: with let swept = smoothstep(0, 1, sweep), a point at angle 2·π·swept and a count floor(24·swept) of the marks it has passed stay together, however the easing changes.
  • show and drop say when marks are there, by name or .tag, and a beat’s block shows what it declares. A mark that’s ever shown isn’t there before it, a dropped one isn’t there after, and while it isn’t there it isn’t drawn at all. A mark no beat names is always there. How it arrives and leaves is the sheet’s, with self.life. A mark that moves during the beat that shows it shouldn’t fade in for the whole beat, since the fade hides the move: with snap on the move and opacity: smoothstep(0, 1, self.life), the mark is half there when 97% of the move is over. Make it solid in the first few frames, opacity: snap(8·self.life), or show it in a beat of its own before it moves.
  • focus says what a beat is about, by name or .tag. It holds until a later beat names something else, and before any does, everything is in focus. A sheet reads it as self.focus.
  • A caption holds until a beat has another, and "" clears it. Captions are drawn in the figure only when a sheet asks, with style caption { … }, since a page can show them as text.
  • A named beat can leave its length out: beat grow show c. With no duration statement it takes a second. Under a stated duration, the beats that wrote no length share evenly what the written lengths and pauses leave of it, and it’s an error if they leave nothing. Either way it’s a move like any other: its name is its progress, and duration counts it. A second is a first guess that nobody wrote, so say for once a move’s timing matters.
  • Moves and steps can’t be mixed in one figure. A name makes a beat a move, so giving each step one is how a figure of steps becomes a figure of moves.

Equations

solve defines unknowns by equations, and they’re then ordinary names:

solve (mu, nu) from 0, exp(pi² / (6·n2)):
  tangency(w, mu, nu) = tangency(w1, mu, nu),
  tangency(one, mu, nu) = tangency(w1, mu, nu)
let k = sqrt(tangency(w, mu, nu))

It runs Newton’s method each frame, using exact symbolic derivatives, on as many unknowns as there are equations.

  • It starts from from every time, with no memory of the last answer, so a frame still depends only on its inputs. Which solution it finds is the start’s business, and the start can use params.
  • No answer means absent. A system that doesn’t settle on a solution, within 50 steps and 1e-9, is absent, so whatever depends on it isn’t drawn, and exists can ask.
  • The unknowns can’t use functions Pencil can’t differentiate. That’s a compile error, and it names the function.

Collections

dots, circles and curves draw one mark many times, once for each combination of their variables. A variable counts in whole numbers and includes both ends of its range, and a later range can use an earlier variable:

dots grid_points = grid(a, b) for a in -q..q, b in -2..q + 2

A variable can count over a list instead, its values in the order written: for s in {-1, 1}, beside ranges as any variable is, for i in 0..n, s in {-1, 1}, with every combination. Its values are numbers or points, with numbers among points as points on the real axis, as a choice param’s options are, and can read an earlier variable: s in {i, -i}. A list needs a value. for s in -1..1 counts -1, 0 and 1, so a list is the way to say the two signs.

± and ∓ draw both branches. Anywhere in a collection’s expressions, its with included, ± makes each instance two, the + branch first, as a last variable that varies fastest: for i in 0..n with a ± is 2(n + 1) instances. Every ± in a statement takes the same sign and every ∓ the opposite, so (±a, ±b) is two points and (±a, ∓b) the other two. Both forms work, ±cosh(t) and a ± b. One with only ∓ is the same two branches in the other order. A collection with a ± and no for is a collection of two:

curves hyp = parametric (t): (±cosh(t), sinh(t)) for t in -2..2

That ± is in what the collection draws. As a whole range, med ± dev is an interval instead (see Curve forms), and a statement can have both: dots d = (k, ±1) for k in 2 ± 1 is k from 1 to 3, two dots for each, the sign fastest.

A style reads which branch an instance is as self.sign, 1 for the first and −1 for the second, wherever it reads the collection’s variables: style hyp { width: 2px + self.sign·1px }. Lists in one expression zip, as Desmos’s do, and a for is for every combination; ± is the only list an expression can hold for now, so there’s no question of lengths. Underneath, a list is a whole-number variable, s.index, and s is the value it picks, as a choice param’s is, and the sign is a list self.sign in {1, -1}. A statement with a ± can’t also name a variable or a with sign, which self.sign could be taken for.

± has two uses, and anywhere else it’s an error. In what a collection draws it’s two branches. As the whole of a range, med ± dev, it’s an interval, drawn once. In a let, a curve’s expression, a param’s default, a bind, a handle, a function or a style it would draw two marks, so the error names the collection to use. In one end of a range it would make two ranges, and as a list’s value, s in {±1}, it would be a variable over the signs, which ± already is, so those errors say to count over the signs as values, s in {1, -1}. In a label’s text it’s the character.

A curve has its own parameter too, which runs smoothly, and comes first. So what Desmos writes as s = [-3...3] / 3 is:

curves across = parametric (t): x0 + s·r / 3 + t·i for t in -r..r for s in -3..3

Its range can read what counts it, and with names can be used in both. curves can go through a map, and a viewport can fit one, which fits all of them. It’s lines, so it has a stroke and no fill, and that stroke can be one color for all of them or one for each (below). Its width can vary per curve, and along each with self.t, and each gets its own dashes and head. Where curves in one collection cross, they don’t darken each other, as they do when they’re separate marks.

  • It’s one mark, so one rule styles it all, and the count can follow a param from frame to frame.
  • with names a value per instance: circles c = circle(z, z + (r, 0)) for a in 0..q with z = spiral(a) works z out once per circle. It can be a number or a point, and can use the names before it.
  • An instance that doesn’t exist is skipped, and one off the frame or too small to see costs nothing further.
  • Sizes can vary per instance: radius and width can use the variables, self.scale, the style pixels per world unit, and for dots, self.x and self.y, where the dot ended up: radius: min(0.3·k·self.x·self.scale·1px, 3px).
  • So can colors: a collection’s stroke, the line of each curve or each circle’s rim, and the fill of dots can use the variables and the with names, so a hue can index a family: style arms { stroke: hue(r / n) }. A color is per instance and not along a line, so a curve’s own parameter isn’t one of them. Where lines of one collection in two colors cover the same pixel, the one that covers more of it shows there, the first drawn of two that cover it alike, so they still don’t darken each other. corpus/017-arm-colors colors a spiral’s arms this way.
  • circles can be circles through three points, so circles c = circle(f(p), f(q), f(s)) for … is what a Möbius map makes of a family. Any of them can be a line this frame, and is drawn as one.
  • Circles have sides, per instance: style c::inside { fill: … }. A side’s fill and fill_opacity can use the variables, the with names, self.dist, self.pixel and self.curvature. Every pixel adds up every circle, so this costs about 0.09 ms per circle at 1080² on an M1 Pro, and it’s limited to 256 per collection, which is an error past that. A collection with only rims doesn’t pay for it and has no limit.
  • A collection is a backdrop: labels don’t try to avoid it.

Panels

A panel is its own view of the figure, with its own marks, its own viewport saying what it looks at, and its own shader. How panels sit is a sheet’s (see Styles). What’s outside any panel is shared, so every panel sees the same params and bindings.

A thing is declared once, and each panel draws it through a map. A group holds things in their own coordinates, and use … through sends them through a function:

fn to_turn(w) = …
let zero = (0, 0)
group edges() {
  curve side = parametric (t): corner·t for t in 0..1
  dot zero
  label name_zero at zero away (-1, 0)
}
panel flat "Lattice" {
  viewport { fit: side }
  use edges()
  text name_zero = "0"
}
panel log "Log space" "T(w) = 2πi·w / A" {
  viewport { fit: side }
  use edges() through above as up
  use edges() through to_turn
  text name_zero = "0"
}
  • What goes through: parametric curves, two-point segments, dots, labels, and dots and curves collections. A segment becomes the map’s image of it, so it can bend. A construction or a circles collection can’t, since the image of a circle isn’t a circle: map a center in its with instead.
  • Only marks move. A let stays what was written, in the group’s coordinates, so one point has one value, and what a panel shows is its image.
  • A label’s away goes through too, exactly, by the map’s derivative at that point. A direction worked out once in the group’s coordinates keeps its side of a curve in every panel, as long as the map doesn’t flip orientation.
  • Maps compose: a group can use another through a map, and the outer one applies last.
  • use … as up draws a group again: what it declares becomes up_side, and each mark is tagged with its plain name and up, so style side reaches every copy and style .up reaches one set.
  • A group’s parameters are values, and they’re its own, so two groups can both have a k.

What a thing is called is up to each panel. label n at P declares where a name goes, and text n = "1" says what it is here, with {expr} for values. A panel with no text for a label doesn’t show it, since that space has no name for it. text for a label that doesn’t exist is a mistake. label n = "P" at P still writes both at once.

After a panel’s title can come a formula, styled by style formula { fill: muted }.

outline o = detail draws the rectangle another panel is looking at, to mark a close-up. radius keeps it big enough to read as a marker, even when what it marks is only a few pixels across.

A mark carries its panel’s name as a tag, so style steps.whole { … } styles it in that panel alone, and style steps styles it in all of them. A rule that names a mark has to find it in at least one panel. style title { fill: ink; size: 14px } styles panel titles. fit can name parametric curves and curves collections as well as points and circles.

Expressions that move

An expression is a list of states, and what’s written the same in two of them moves from one to the other. There are two ways to say when, and a figure picks by what drives it.

Named beats, for a derivation that’s told. Each state says on the beat that brings it, and writes what that beat changes:

pause 0.5
beat write for 0.8
pause 1
beat measure for 0.5
pause 1
beat expand for 0.8
pause 1
beat factor for 0.6
pause 1
beat answer for 0.8

place equation = (0, 1)
place result = (0, 0)

expression work {
  on write: "z ( a + b )" at equation
  on expand: "z a + z.1 b" at equation
  on factor: "z ( a + b )" at equation
  on answer: "= c" at result
}
  • A state is where its beat ends. The expression starts from what it held, moves through the beat, holds what’s written as the beat ends, and keeps it until the next beat a state names. Before the first, it’s empty.
  • A state writes the places it changes. A place it names is set to what’s written there, so a term that was at that place and isn’t written now goes, as z.1 does on factor. A place it doesn’t name keeps what it has: answer writes at result, and the equation stays above it without being written again.
  • A term is in one place, so a term written at a new place moves there and leaves the place it was at, which is then empty if that was all it held. on join: "a + b" at sum takes a and b from wherever they were.
  • empty clears every place: on clear: empty. There’s no way yet to clear one place and keep the rest, since no figure has needed it, and writing nothing at a place, "" at p, is an error and not a way to do it.
  • A beat no state names changes nothing, so a hold isn’t written: measure above can show an angle, and take as long as it likes, while the algebra stays put. Making a beat longer, or putting a pause or another beat between two states, retimes the story and leaves which terms move alone.
  • States are written in the order their beats run, and each beat brings one state. A state out of order, a beat named twice, and a name that isn’t a beat’s are errors at that state’s line: `factor` comes before `expand` in the timeline, but follows it in `work`. The beats can be written above the expression or below it, a beat with a block too: its terms are drawn where the expression is written.
  • on takes a beat’s name, which a move has when it’s written with one, with a length or without. A step, beat "caption" { … }, has none, so a figure of steps drives its expression by beat, as below.

A number, for scrubbing. by takes any number, and a state is written for each whole value from 1: at 3.4 the expression is on its way from state 3 to state 4. State 0 is the empty one before the first that’s written, and empty writes another. A param a reader drags is the usual driver, as here, where each state is one more term of a series and n can drive the curve it approximates too:

param n = 1 in 1..4

place sum = (0, 1)

expression series by n {
  "1" at sum
  "1 + x" at sum
  "1 + x +.1 x²/2" at sum
  "1 + x +.1 x²/2 +.2 x³/6" at sum
}

With by, each state is written whole: what a state doesn’t write isn’t there. by beat is a state for every beat, in order, with a state that holds written again. by a sum of beats’ names is what on works out, how many of those beats are done and how far the one that’s moving has come, and on builds the same whole states, each from the one before and what its beat writes. pencil ir lists them, which is where to read what an expression holds on a beat.

Terms are separated by spaces. Nothing is diffed: identity is what’s written. So 2ab is one term and 2 a b is three. If the next state writes b somewhere else, the spaced b moves there and the rest stays, and the joined 2ab has nothing in the next state, so it fades out while 2a and b fade in (web/terms.html shows the two side by side).

  • The same term in the next state moves to its new spot, and stays solid.
  • A new term fades in, and a term that’s gone fades out, riding along with its neighbors.
  • A new term beside one that travels is solid within the first few frames of the move, so it’s seen riding along: the a of z.1 a goes out with the copy of z. A fade as long as the move would show it only once it had arrived. A new term that stays where it is, as when 2ab gives way to 2a in the same place, fades in with the step.
  • A copy is written z.1, and prints as z. When it’s new, it starts on z.
  • A term is in one place, so a state can’t write the same one twice: a + b +.1 c has two plus signs. A number can’t have a copy yet, since 2.1 is a number.
  • A term can have a name: slow:2ab prints 2ab, and is the term slow. The name is what moves between states and what a copy is written from, slow.1:2ab, and it’s a tag, so style .slow { … } and focus .slow reach the term together with an arrow tagged slow. One name ties a symbol to its geometry. A name prints one text, so slow:2ba in another state is an error.
  • When a copy goes, it moves into a term of the same name at the same place: factoring.

Each term is a mark named work.z.1, with the tags term, work and z, so style term.a { fill: blue } colors every a. A term is mathematics, so it’s laid out as a label’s $…$ is, whatever its font, and x^2 as a term has a real exponent (see Mathematics in labels). Core says where each term goes.

Mathematics in labels

$…$ in a label’s text is mathematics, laid out: "area = $x^2/2$" is the words, then x squared over two. Inside a span the notation is Pencil’s own, the one a let is written in, with parentheses to group. It isn’t TeX, and there’s no backslash.

Written Drawn
x^2, x^(n + 1), e^(iπ), x^-1 A superscript. Parentheses that only group aren’t drawn. x² is the same as x^2.
x_1, x_(i + 1), a_n^2 A subscript, and both together. x1 and x₁ are x_1, as they are in an expression.
x^2/2, (a + b)/2, 1/2π A fraction. The bar takes the product before it and the factors right after it, so 1/2π is 1 over 2π and 1/2 x is a half, times x, as Pencil computes them. Parentheses the bar makes unnecessary aren’t drawn.
sqrt(x + 1), √2, √(x + 1) A root, with its bar over what it holds.
abs(z) |z|.
(1/2)^2 Brackets as tall as what they hold.
sin x, arg z, ln(x), lim, det, gcd A function’s name upright, a thin space from what it’s of. These are Pencil’s functions and a few more names mathematics sets upright.
a + b = c, z ↦ z^2, f: ℝ → ℝ, -7 Operators and relations spaced as TeX spaces them, however the source is spaced. A hyphen is a minus, and * is ·.
  • Letters are variables, in italics, and letters written together stay together, so 2ab reads as it does in a product. Digits, operators, brackets and capital Greek are upright.
  • {expr} is a value in a span as it is outside one, since a span groups with parentheses and never braces: "$z^{n}$" is z to whatever n is this frame. What the value prints is laid out too, so a polar point’s e^(2πi/3) has a real exponent.
  • A fraction stacks at the label’s own size. Inside a superscript or a subscript, or inside another fraction, it stays on the line with a slash, where a stacked one would be too small to read. ∕ (U+2215) or ÷ keeps one on the line anywhere.
  • Some text is mathematics without being marked: an expression’s terms, and what a label writes about a value, its name, expr and value. They’re laid out as a span is, whatever the label’s font, which only sets its words. A value written into a label’s own words, as "+{q}", is part of the words.
  • A dollar sign is $$, and a $ that nothing closes is an error.
  • What it can’t typeset: matrices, lines aligned on their =, limits above and below a ∑ or ∫ (they sit beside it, as a subscript and a superscript), accents such as hats, bars and vector arrows, and bold. A tall root or bracket is the font’s glyph made taller, not a larger one drawn for the size, so its strokes thicken a little.

The command and a page draw one layout. The core places every glyph and rule from the metrics of the math font they both draw with, so a formula is the same in a video, in a poster and live on a page, and the label’s size, which placement and leaders use, is the layout’s.

Typing the symbols. Pencil’s text is the symbol itself: →, θ, ℝ. The playground’s editor writes them for a keyboard that lacks them. A LaTeX name after a backslash becomes its symbol when it’s finished by a space, by anything else that can’t continue it, or by Tab: \to → →, \theta → θ, \R → ℝ, \nabla → ∇, \le → ≤, \in → ∈, \infty → ∞, \partial → ∂, \mapsto → ↦, \times → ×, \pm → ±, and the rest of LaTeX’s Greek, relations, arrows and set symbols (formula::symbols in the core has the list). Inside a label’s text, ->, |->, <=, >=, !=, ~= and +- become →, ↦, ≤, ≥, ≠, ≈ and ±. Undo gives back what was typed. Nothing in a file is ever read that way: a .pen holds the symbols, so an agent or a script writes them directly.

Expressions

Numbers, names, + - * / ^, ± and ∓ (in a collection’s expressions, two branches, see Collections; as a whole range, med ± dev, an interval, see Curve forms), · for multiply, ² and ³, unary -, and calls. Factors side by side multiply, as 2π, 2(x + 1), (a + b)(a - b) and a b. Right against each other they bind tighter than /, so 1/2π is 1/(2π). A space ends that: 1/2 π is π/2, and (k - 1)/N π is the quotient times π, as it reads in Desmos, where the fraction’s bar stops. A product doesn’t reach past the end of its line or a word that follows an expression, such as for, in, step or tag. A function’s name before ( is a call. Any other name there multiplies the parentheses, so π(t - 1) and a (b + c) are products, and a power after them is the parentheses’ own: a(b + c)² is a·(b + c)². Letters together are one name, so ab is a name and a b is a product. The constants’ own glyphs π, ℯ, ⅈ and ⅇ never join a name, so 2πi, 2πr and iπ are products, and π_1 is still a name. (a, b) is a point, which is also a complex number (see below), and P.x and P.y read one. Names can be Unicode. A subscript is part of a name, and x1, x_1, x₁ and x_{1} are all the name x_1, as in Desmos and LaTeX; digits inside a name, as in p2q, aren’t one. time is always available. duration is the number the figure’s duration statement says, so bind theta = mod(time, duration) / duration·2·π turns once a pass and the length is written once. In a figure with no statement whose beats are moves (see Beats), it’s what the beats and pauses add up to, which is how long the figure runs: pause 0.5, beat grow for 1 and beat spin for 2 make duration 3.5, read above them or below, and a named beat that wrote no length counts its second. It reads the same in a let, a bind, a mark and a style, and it’s a constant, but not in its own statement, and not in a beat’s length or a pause of a figure whose beats add up to it, directly or through a let: that length would be part of the sum it reads, and the error says so. A figure with no statement and no moves, which has no beats, pauses alone, or steps, has no duration, and reading it is an error. One whose beats have blocks reads it after them, or says its duration. A figure says its duration once, and once it does, nothing else at its top level can take the name: a second statement, or a let, param, choice, fn, solve unknown or beat called duration, is an error. A parameter is local as always, so a fn or group whose parameter is called duration reads its own argument, and a sheet’s own let duration is the sheet’s. A figure with no duration statement can take the name for its own value, as with pi. pi and π are π, and e and ℯ are Euler’s number, unless the figure takes the name for something of its own, as bounds does with its curve e; then every e in the figure is that, and exp is Euler’s. In the IR they’re MathJSON’s Pi and ExponentialE. 2e is 2·e, while 2e3 is 2000. Coordinates only exist inside the curve that names them.

Points add and subtract, scale by a number, and negate. All of this expands to scalars at compile time, so the IR stays symbolic and bindings are evaluated once per frame.

Constants

duration, a pause, a beat’s length, a param’s step, a poster’s values, and a viewport’s bounds and pad each hold for the whole figure, so each has to be a constant. A constant is a number, a constant such as π, duration, or a let or a call to the figure’s own fn made only of those, written anywhere in the figure:

let period = 12
duration period
bind theta = mod(time, period) / period·2·π

A param’s range is the one place that can also follow params: an end may read params directly, and apart from them it has to be constant, so a let it reads has to be a constant one.

Anything that can change isn’t a constant, even where it hasn’t yet: time, a param, though it has a default, a choice, beat and a beat’s name, a solve’s unknowns, and a let that reads any of them. The error names it, and what a let depends on: `duration` must be constant, and `period` depends on the param `a`.

A constant is a finite number, since nothing that draws a figure can take anything else: duration 0/0, pause 1/0 and poster { time: (1, 2) } are errors. duration is more: a number above 0, so duration 0 is an error too. A pause and a beat’s length can’t be below 0, a step has to be above 0, and a viewport’s bounds have to increase.

MathJSON

Expressions compile to MathJSON, and where Pencil has something MathJSON names, it uses MathJSON’s name, as the Compute Engine does: imag(z) is Imaginary, conj(z) is Conjugate, arctanh is Artanh. So are the constants, which are defaults (above): a figure that takes the name gets its own value.

Written MathJSON Value
pi, π Pi π
e, ℯ, ⅇ ExponentialE Euler’s number. e^w is exp(w), for a complex w too, so e^(iπ) + 1 is 0.
i, ⅈ ImaginaryUnit The point (0, 1), which compiles away.
GoldenRatio GoldenRatio (1 + √5)/2. Not φ, which is an angle as often.
EulerGamma, CatalanConstant, Degrees the same γ, Catalan’s constant, and π/180, so 30·Degrees is 30° in radians.

Where Pencil differs on purpose:

  • Names are words, so eps is one name, where the Compute Engine’s LaTeX reads it as e·p·s. A space splits a product: e p s. Nothing splits by what happens to be defined, as GeoGebra does, where a half-typed ToCo quietly becomes T, o and C: an unknown name is an error. Only the constants’ glyphs split, and they’re fixed.
  • A document has one scope. The Compute Engine substitutes a constant as it parses, so a variable named e has to be declared before anything that uses it. A figure’s let e applies to every e in it, wherever it’s written.
  • exp(x) stays Exp. The Compute Engine’s canonical form is ["Power", "ExponentialE", x], which means the same, and Pencil turns that into Exp, so derivatives and complex values take one path.

Pasting LaTeX

The playground and the AST page read LaTeX pasted from Desmos or MathLive as Pencil text (latex.rs), and say what it became. Undo takes it back. Text with a backslash, a ^{, or a leading $ is LaTeX, and Pencil text never has them.

Pasted Becomes
y=\frac{1}{2}x^{2} y = 1/2·x^2
\frac{1}{2\pi}, -\frac{b}{2a} 1/(2π), -b/(2a)
\exponentialE^{\imaginaryI\pi}+1 e^(iπ) + 1
\theta_{1}, x_{1}y θ_1, x_1·y
xy, 2\pi r x·y, 2πr
`\left z\right
\sin x\cos x, \sin^{2}x sin(x)·cos(x), sin(x)^2
30^{\circ} 30·Degrees
  • Letters run together are a product, as LaTeX means them, so xy comes out x·y, not the name xy. A longer name has to be \operatorname{…} or \mathrm{…} in LaTeX, and is one name here too.
  • A letter before parentheses is a call only if it’s a function: a built-in, a fn in the document, or the one a line defines, as f\left(x\right)=x^{2}. Otherwise it multiplies, so a\left(x+1\right) is a·(x + 1), as Desmos reads it.
  • Brackets go only where Pencil needs them, with one more: a product in a denominator, 1/(2π), which Pencil would read the same way without them but a reader might not.
  • \phi and \varphi are both φ, and \epsilon and \varepsilon both ε: the letter a keyboard types, whichever way LaTeX draws it.
  • Lines pasted together are one graph: a function any line defines, as G\left(u,v\right)=u+v, is a call on every line. Three or more things in parentheses are arguments whatever the name is, since a point has two coordinates.
  • Desmos’s own spellings read as what they mean: A.x and A.y stay, P.\operatorname{real} is real(P), \tan^{-1} is arctan, and \log is base 10 while \log_{2}x is ln(x)/ln(2).
  • A function LaTeX has and Pencil doesn’t yet keeps its name, as \gcd, \lcm, \det and \lg do, so the figure’s error names it. pencil latex writes such a line as a comment that says which.
  • \pm and \mp are ± and ∓, as (-b ± sqrt(b^2 - 4a·c))/(2a) and x = 5 ± 2, and a sign before a product brackets it, ±(2x). Where the text goes decides whether Pencil takes it: in what a collection draws it’s two branches, as a whole range an interval, and anywhere else the figure’s error says why.
  • What has no Pencil form is an error, and the LaTeX pastes as written: Desmos’s piecewise braces, with and for, comparisons, lists, derivatives, an n-th root (x^(1/n) differs from it for negative x), 3D points, and infinity.

Numbers

Function Meaning
sqrt(x), exp(x), ln(x), abs(x), sign(x) The usual. sign(0) is 0.
log(x), log(x, b) The logarithm to base 10, as LaTeX’s \log and Desmos’s are, or to base b. The natural one is ln(x).
floor(x), ceil(x), round(x) The whole number below, above and nearest. A half rounds away from 0, so round(-2.5) is −3.
sin(x), cos(x), tan(x), sec(x), csc(x), cot(x) Radians. 30·Degrees is an angle in degrees.
arcsin(x), arccos(x), arctan(x), or asin(x), acos(x), atan(x) Their inverses, in radians. arctan is between −π/2 and π/2.
arcsec(x), arccsc(x), arccot(x) arccos(1/x), arcsin(1/x), and for arccot the angle between 0 and π, as Desmos has it, so it has no jump at 0.
atan2(y, x) The angle of the point (x, y), between −π and π.
arcsinh(x), arccosh(x), arccoth(x), or arsinh(x), arcosh(x), arcoth(x) The inverses of the hyperbolic functions, with arctanh(x), which are under Complex numbers.
min(a, b), max(a, b), clamp(x, lo, hi) Limits.
mod(x, y) Floored, so the result takes y’s sign.
mix(a, b, t) a at 0 and b at 1. Also mixes two colors, in linear light.
smoothstep(a, b, t) 0 before a, 1 after b, eased between.
reveal(age, now, later) 0 before a beat, now during it, later after it.
snap(x), snap(x, power) 0 at or before 0, and 1 at or after 1: gets there fast, then eases in. power defaults to 5.
timeline(time, start, end, …) Which step of a list of moves a time is in: whole while holding, and between two, linearly, while moving.

Points in space

(x, y, z) is a point in space. A mark draws it looking down z, which comes toward the reader, so it’s drawn at its x and y, and a figure that never writes a z is the same figure it was. The view is orthographic: nothing gets smaller with distance.

  • It’s a vector, and not a complex number. It adds to and subtracts from another, scales by a number, and has .x, .y and .z. Multiplying two, or passing one to exp, is an error. A function can build one from a point in the plane: fn rolled(w) = (w.x, r·sin(w.y), r·cos(w.y)).
  • Any mark can take one where it takes a point: a dot, a curve’s point, a segment’s ends, a label’s place.
  • A viewport’s yaw turns the view about its vertical axis, so z comes round toward x: a point is drawn at x·cos(yaw) + z·sin(yaw), and its y.
  • A sheet can read a point’s z, as self.z, along a curve or curves of points in space, in width and opacity, and for each of a collection of dots, in radius. It’s the z the figure wrote, before the view turns. So a figure that puts a tube’s axis at z = 0 has its far side at z < 0, and its sheet can say opacity: mix(0.25, 1, smoothstep(-0.04, 0.04, self.z)). Where that changes along a curve, the stroke is cut there, to a quarter of a pixel, and not at the nearest sample, so the cut moves evenly as the figure does.
  • Nothing is hidden behind anything. Marks are drawn in the order they’re written, as in the plane. Where strokes of one curve or one collection overlap, the one with more ink shows, so a faded far side never dims a near side that crosses it.

corpus/013-tube is the example. Not built: a view that pitches or that a reader turns by dragging, self.z on segments, polygons and single dots, a color that follows depth, and drawing by depth.

Points and constructions

Function Meaning
length(P), dist(A, B), dot(A, B) Numbers from points. length(P) is abs(P), MathJSON’s Abs.
midpoint(A, B) Halfway between.
circle(C, T) About C through T. Fields .x, .y, .r. Its disk is its negative side.
circle(A, B, C) Through three points, in order (below). Fields .a, which is its signed curvature, and .x, .y, .r, which don’t exist on a line.
flip(c) The same circle running the other way round, so its sides trade signs.
line(A, B), ray(A, B) Through two points. A ray starts at A. Two points in one place make no line.
perpendicular(P, l) The line through P at right angles to l.
intersect(u, v, which) Where lines, rays and circles meet, if they do (below). which is 0 or 1, and defaults to 0.
mirror(s, across) A point across a line or point, or a circle across a line.
exists(v) 1 if all of v exists this frame, and 0 if not.
otherwise(v, fallback) v, or all of fallback where v doesn’t exist. They must be the same kind.

A circle through three points has a handedness. Going counterclockwise, its negative side is its disk, and its curvature is positive. Going clockwise, its negative side is everything else, and its curvature is negative. Three points in a line are a line, which runs through 0 curvature without any value going to infinity, and has no center or radius. Two points in one place make no circle.

which names a root, not a place among the points that remain. Along a line, 0 and 1 are in order of its direction. For two circles, 0 is left of the line from the first center to the second. A ray only has the points ahead of its start, so from inside a circle only its root 1 exists, and root 0 is absent, rather than root 1 taking its place and jumping.

Complex numbers

A point is a complex number. (x, y) and x + y·i are the same value, there’s no second type, and i is the point (0, 1):

let omega = -1 / 2 + sqrt(3) / 2·i
fn to_turn(w) = 2·π·i·w / A
fn spiral(t) = exp(t)
  • A number is a point on the real axis, wherever a point is wanted, so curve c = parametric (t): -t for t in 0..q, label n = "1" at 1, circle(0, 1) and 1 + omega all work, and a number answers .x and .y.
  • Arithmetic is complex: · and / between two points multiply and divide them as complex numbers, and +, - and scaling are what they were. dot(a, b) is still the dot product.
  • Powers: z² and z^-3 multiply out, up to a power of 8. Anything else, such as z^2.5 or z^i, is exp(w·ln(z)), on the principal branch.
  • Functions: real(z), imag(z), conj(z), abs(z) and arg(z) read it. exp, ln and sqrt take one too, with principal values. ln(0) and arg(0) don’t exist, and a figure with one draws what it can (see below).
  • The trigonometric functions and their inverses take one too, all of those under Numbers but atan2, floor, ceil and round, on the principal branches, as does log. A number stays a number: arcsin(2) has no answer, as sqrt(-1) has none, and arcsin(2 + 0·i) is complex. On a branch cut the value is the one a formula gives there: arcsin(z) is -i·ln(i·z + sqrt(1 - z²)).
  • Hyperbolic functions: sinh(x), cosh(x), tanh(x), coth(x), sech(x), csch(x) and arctanh(x) (or artanh(x)) take numbers and complex numbers. They compile to exp and ln, and the functions added to them compile the same way, to ones every renderer already has, so a derivative sees through each.
  • i gives way to anything named i, so for i in 1..q still counts, and inside it i is the count. It’s clearer to use another name there. It also means a stray i outside a loop isn’t an unknown name any more.
  • Exact derivatives see through all of it, so solve and a label’s away work on complex values. It all compiles to plain numbers, so a shader and an evaluator don’t know it’s there.

When a value doesn’t exist

Geometry is partial, so a value can be absent on some frames. Only constructions make one:

  • A line or ray that misses a circle, or a circle that’s apart from, inside or the same as another.
  • Parallel lines.
  • A point behind the start of a ray.
  • A line through two points in one place, or a rightangle with a side of no length.

Touching counts as meeting, within rounding, so a tangent by construction doesn’t flicker.

Whatever is built from an absent value is absent too, and only exists and otherwise can see the difference. What that means for each thing that uses one:

Use When its value is absent
A mark Isn’t drawn, along with its label, which pages must then hide.
A style value Hides the mark. To respond instead, let shown = exists(P) and use shown.
A parametric curve’s point Leaves a gap there, and the curve can come in pieces.
A region’s boundary Hides the region: with a gap it doesn’t enclose anything.
fit Skips it, and if nothing is left, uses the declared x and y.
handle Can’t be grabbed. An inverse with no answer leaves its param where it is, and a handle’s other param still moves.
paper A compile error: there has to be something to draw on.
A curve’s field Has to name the value with let first: a field runs per pixel, and existence is decided per frame.

On a page, player.value reads an absent binding as NaN.

Colors

Function Meaning
oklch(l, c, h) Perceptual, with h in degrees.
rgb(r, g, b) sRGB, 0 to 255.
hue(k) A perceptual ramp, with k from 0 to 1 once around.
white, black Names.

Styles

style selector, selector { property: value; … }. Later rules win, across files, with the document’s own rules last. There’s no specificity (SPEC/15). Any property can be none, which takes back what an earlier rule set, as in CSS: after style ray { dash: 10px }, style base { dash: none } draws that one ray solid. stroke: none and fill: none say more: no paint, as in SVG, so stroke: none draws no line and nothing draws one by default (see What’s drawn with nothing said).

A style sheet can name values with let ink = rgb(28, 27, 25). The last sheet to define a name decides what it means everywhere, including in rules written before it, as a CSS variable does. So corpus/theme.style holds a theme’s colors and label roles, and corpus/dark.style only redefines the colors. A name can use another defined in any order, but not itself. A sheet can define functions too, as a document can: fn glow(d, w) = exp(-d / w), then opacity: glow(self.dist, 6px). A call is inlined, its parameters hide the sheet’s names of the same spelling, the last sheet to define a function decides what it means, and a function can’t call itself. A document picks a role by tag: label n = "|z|" at M tag note, and it never picks a number. A rule that names a mark has to find it, but a rule by type or tag may match nothing, since a shared sheet can’t know what each figure uses.

Selectors combine a name or type with tags: c, circle, .aux, circle.blue, and c::inside for a facet. control and q.control are params’ controls (see Controls and readouts). A mark’s type is one of its tags: circle, line, ray, curve, segment, decoration, region, dot, label, arrow, term, dots, circles, curves, outline. paper is the background.

Facets are the two sides of a mark. ::negative and ::positive are the field’s sign. On a circle, ::inside and ::outside are its true disk and everything else, whichever way round it runs, and on a line, where there’s no disk, they follow the sign. Where both name the same part of the plane, ::inside and ::outside win. On anything else that has sides, ::inside and ::outside are aliases for the sign, with the negative side inside.

So a circle through three points that turns over straightens into a line and comes back with its sides’ signs where they were, and its disk on the other one. Style ::negative and the plane doesn’t flash, and style ::inside and the color stays with the disk. A style can tell which it is from self.curvature.

Values are expressions, so they can use time, duration (see Expressions), params and bindings. A few more names exist only here:

Name Meaning
self.dist Distance to the mark, in fill, stroke and fill_opacity, on marks that have one, and negative inside. It’s a true distance: an implicit curve’s is measured to the curve as traced in view, so cos(24·self.dist) makes even bands. A parametric curve has one for its stroke and opacity when its stroke is drawn per pixel, with draw: field: the distance to the curve as sampled, with no sign, since such a curve has no sides.
self.pixel How big a device pixel is in world units, wherever self.dist is, so that a glow can be a number of the screen’s pixels across. It’s what the screen can resolve, not the design: 1px is a device pixel only at the design size on a 1× screen.
self.curvature A circle’s signed curvature: above 0 counterclockwise, below 0 clockwise, and 0 on a line.
self.t Position along a stroke, 0 to 1, in width, and in a curve’s opacity.
self.z A point’s third coordinate as the figure wrote it: along a curve of points in space, in width and opacity, and for each dot of a collection of them, in radius. See Points in space.
self.sign Which branch of a collection with ± an instance is: 1 for the first, where ± is +, and −1 for the second. Wherever the collection’s variables can be read. See Collections.
self.age See Beats.
self.life How present the mark is, from 0 before a beat shows it to 1, and back to 0 as one drops it, moving with those beats. 1 for a mark no beat names.
self.focus How much the beats are about the mark, from 0 to 1, changing as a beat that names something moves. 1 until a beat names anything.

A length is in one of three units, and they’re all lengths, so they mix: width: 1px + 0.01, and self.dist / 1px is a distance in design pixels.

Unit Is Scales with
a bare number The figure’s own units, as in the document. width: 0.02 is that wide in the plane, so it grows as a fit zooms in. The math
px A design pixel, as SVG’s px is inside a viewBox. style figure { width } says how many there are across. The figure as it’s drawn
em The reader’s text size. On a page, the page’s font size where the figure is, so text matches the text around it at any size the figure is drawn. A reader who changes their text size changes it, and the labels follow at once, so a page sets its text in rem, not px. In a video, style figure { em }, 17 px by default. The reader’s text

Text goes in em, as the theme’s does, and strokes, dots and arrows in px. A figure’s own size and a panel’s are design pixels, so they can’t be in em.

Colors can be scaled and added: white·4, mix(a, b, t) + c / 3. They aren’t clipped until the end, and rgb can go past 255. sinh, cosh and tanh also work in a style. So a glow reads fill_opacity: tanh(2·self.pixel / abs(self.dist)).

Property Applies to Meaning
fill Regions, dots, labels, facets A color, or none for no fill. A field’s fill needs a facet, and so does a circles collection’s, fill: none included, since they’re filled only by their sides. A label, a term, a panel’s title or formula, or the caption with fill: none isn’t drawn. The paper can’t be none: leave its fill out for white.
fill_opacity Anything filled Scales only the fill, on top of opacity.
stroke Curves, lines, regions, dots A color, or none for no line. A collection’s can be a color for each of its instances (see Collections).
width Strokes A length. Can vary along the stroke with self.t, and with self.z on a curve of points in space.
head, head_span Curves With head: 13px, a curve ends in an arrowhead. head_span: 1 holds it to 60% of the last 1 of the curve’s parameter, so it can’t dwarf a spiral’s tight turns.
dash, gap Lines Lengths. A loop gets a whole number of dashes, stretched to fit. dash: 0, like dash: none, is solid.
cap Lines butt (default) or round.
draw Strokes A hint: auto (default), line or field. field draws an implicit or a parametric curve’s stroke per pixel from its distance, so a parametric curve’s stroke and opacity can fall off with self.dist: draw: field; width: 8; stroke: white; opacity: tanh(2·self.pixel / abs(self.dist)) is a line of light. A stroke drawn that way has no dashes, taper or trim.
blend Edges, sides gamma (default, as SVG does), linear, or add, which adds to what’s there in display values and never covers it.
tone paper clip (default) or tanh, which runs the finished picture through tanh in display values, so that what blend: add piles up stays in range. Or a number from 0 to 1 between them, which can change, so a figure can turn into one that adds light: tone: glow with a beat named glow.
opacity Any mark Scales the whole mark. On a curve or curves it can vary along the stroke, with self.t and self.z: each part of the stroke has that much ink, and where parts overlap the most ink shows.
ticks, tick Segments How many short marks cross its middle, saying it’s as long as another with as many, and how long each is, 10 px by default. Drawn in its stroke without its dashes, once a trimmed segment reaches its middle.
leader, leader_gap Labels A line from its point to its text, this wide, in the text’s color. It starts leader_gap from the point, so it can meet a ring, and stops a little short of the text, wherever the label settles.
radius Dots, circles, outlines A length. A dot’s size, a cap on a collection’s circles, or an outline’s least half-size.
size Labels A length, usually in em. Defaults to 1 em.
halo Labels Its full width, in the paper’s color.
font Labels A role: sans (default) or math, an italic for names and notes. Both are the package’s own fonts, Libertinus Sans and Libertinus Serif Italic, the same files in the command and on a page, with Libertinus Math behind each for the symbols a text face lacks and for a label’s mathematics. It sets a label’s words: its mathematics is laid out the same in either.
place Labels settle (default), tied to its offset by a spring and pushed off what’s drawn and other labels, or fixed, exactly at its offset. A label written on its own point, as label z at z is, starts a little up and to the right of it, and settles from there.
format Labels How a point in its text is written: point (default) as (−0.50, −0.87), complex as −0.50 − 0.87i, or polar as e^(−2πi/3), with an angle that’s a fraction of π up to twelfths written as one. A point and a complex number are one thing in Pencil, so which it reads as is the sheet’s.
kind Controls Which control a param gets: slider, radios, select or checkbox (see Controls and readouts).
text Labels, controls What a label says about the value it’s about, as parts joined by =: caption (its own words, or the value’s name if it has none), name, expr (the expression as written: a let’s right side, or what’s between the braces) and value. text: expr = value is σ(2) = −0.50 − 0.87i, text: name = value is root = −0.50 − 0.87i, and text: caption is the words alone. Parts that come out the same are said once, so a param’s expr = value is q = 3. Without it, a label says its own words, or its value if it has none. A label that isn’t about one value says its words whatever this is. A readout with none says which value it is (see Controls and readouts). On a control, what it says (see Controls and readouts).
digits Labels How many decimal places its values are written to. Defaults to 2. A whole number is written whole, and a part that rounds to zero is left out of a complex number.
head Arrows The head’s length. Defaults to 14 px.
distance Labels How far a label written with away sits from its point. Defaults to 16/17 em.
show Any mark Draws it only while this is above 0, decided per frame. Can also read view.width, the view’s width in world units, for zoom levels.
trim Curves, lines, arrows, circles How much of the stroke is drawn, from its start: 0 to 1 of a curve’s parameter, or of a straight line’s length. An arrow grows from its tail. A circle starts due east of its center and runs counterclockwise, and is drawn as a line to be trimmed. A collection of curves can trim each one with its variables. A traced curve, a region, dots and circles in a collection have no start, so they can’t.

What’s drawn with nothing said

A figure with no sheet shows its marks. After the sheets are applied, a mark that would paint nothing gets its type’s default paint, in the default ink:

Mark Default paint
curve, circle, line, ray, segment, decoration, arrow, curves, circles, outline A stroke, 1 px wide, with butt caps. An arrow’s head is 14 px.
region Its outline, as a stroke.
dot, dots A fill, 3 px in radius.
label, term Its text in the ink. A label settles, so label z at z moves off its dot; it’s otherwise as it is with nothing said: sans, 1 em, no halo. A term keeps its place in its expression.
  • A mark that paints anything is left as written. A side’s fill counts, so c::inside { fill: blue } alone draws no line around c. A fill on a mark that never draws one, such as a segment, doesn’t count, so the segment still gets its stroke.
  • What a sheet does write picks the paint and is kept, on a mark it applies to. Alone, these ask for a stroke: width on any mark, a dot too, so style c { width: 3px } is a 3 px line in the ink; dash and gap on anything but a dot or dots; head on a curve, curves or an arrow; head_span on a curve or curves; and trim, ticks and tick, which are only taken where they apply. radius asks a dot or dots for a fill, and fill_opacity a dot or a region. Anything else, such as a radius on a region, asks for nothing, and the mark gets its type’s own paint.
  • stroke: none and fill: none keep that paint off, and a mark is hidden by writing none for its default paint: stroke: none for a line, fill: none for a dot. stroke: none on a dot that has nothing else still fills it, as SVG’s would. show: 0 makes a mark absent instead, so labels don’t settle around it.
  • Text takes the ink too: a label, a term, a panel’s title and its formula with no fill, and the caption.
  • The ink is the sheets’ ink, if one names a color that, as corpus/theme.style does, and a sheet’s ink that isn’t a color is an error. Otherwise it’s black or white, whichever contrasts more with the paper, by WCAG’s contrast ratio: black on the default white paper. A paper that changes is judged frame by frame, so the ink turns over when the paper’s luminance passes about 0.18.

A figure as SVG

pencil svg DOC.pen --style … --out FIGURE.svg writes one frame as vector graphics, for a paper, a slide or a drawing program. It’s the poster’s moment unless --t or --param say another, at the figure’s design size unless --size does. A param that follows time is set by one or the other: --param holds it, --t gives it the value it has at that time, and both for the same param is an error. It is written from the lines, regions and label places a frame prepares for the renderers, so it matches pencil render of the same frame. Each mark is an element, or a group of them, with the mark’s name as its id, and a label is text.

A style has a vector form when its value is one color or one number for a whole mark, for one of a collection, or along a stroke. What’s worked out per pixel has none. That part is left out, and a line on stderr names each mark and the property, so nothing is drawn as something it isn’t.

In a sheet In the SVG
stroke with width, dash, gap, cap, trim, ticks A path with that stroke. A curve is the short straight pieces it’s traced in, flat to a small fraction of a pixel at the size it’s written for.
head, and an arrow The stroke, and a triangle for its head.
A width that varies along the stroke, with self.t or self.z The stroke’s outline, as a filled shape. With a dash as well it’s left out, for now.
An opacity that varies along the stroke A mask over the stroke’s color, lighter where there’s more ink.
fill and fill_opacity on a region, a dot, the sides of a circle or of a curve that closes inside the frame, and each circle of a collection A filled shape. The side of a curve that leaves the frame is left out, for now.
opacity, show, radius As drawn.
A label, with size, font, halo, leader and where place put it <text> centered on its place, in the fonts a page draws labels in, over the same text stroked in the paper’s color for its halo. A viewer with another font moves only the glyphs.
A fill, fill_opacity or stroke that reads self.dist That fill or stroke is left out, and the rest of the mark is drawn.
blend: add The mark is left out: SVG has no paint that adds light.
blend: linear Drawn, as gamma, which is how SVG blends.
tone on paper Not applied. Colors are as their styles give them, so what a tanh would have dimmed is brighter.

A figure’s size is a sheet’s, and so is how panels are laid out. These values hold for the whole figure, so they can’t read a param, and a rule for a panel that doesn’t exist is a mistake. All panels have to be one size, for now.

Rule Property Meaning
style figure width, height In px, a figure’s design size, for one without panels. With width, px sizes scale with the output, as an SVG’s do with its viewBox, and without it a px is a CSS pixel. With both, they give its shape, and without height the shape is its viewport’s. A page sizes the figure’s canvas to its column, keeping that shape.
em In px, how big an em is where there’s no page to say, as in a video. Defaults to 17.
style panels columns How many columns. Defaults to 1.
gap In px, between panels.
title In px, the band above each panel for its title.
style panel, style panel.whole width, height In px, a panel’s design size. Defaults to 400.

A beat’s caption is drawn by one more rule, and only when a sheet has it, centered along the bottom of the canvas. As a beat with a new caption starts to move, the old one fades out and then the new one fades in, each over a fifth of a second, or less if the move is shorter.

Rule Property Meaning
style caption fill, size, halo As a label’s. size defaults to 18 px.
font sans (default) or math.
distance From the bottom of the canvas to the caption’s center. Defaults to 28 px.
pad How much room a fit leaves around what it fits, as a fraction of its size. Defaults to 0.1.

Pencil is early, and its syntax will change. Source on GitHub, under the MIT license.
